name: Green Apple
lede: Green apple is a vivid yellowish green named for tart fruit; as a color name it is recent, but the apple-green it echoes is old.

sections.title: Name and meaning
sections.body:
*Green apple* is a food word turned into a color name: the green of an unripe or tart apple. In our sources it has no long record. The earliest entry we can document is the xkcd color survey of 2010, where it names a vivid yellowish green [1]. Who first used it as a color name is undocumented.

The older, related term is *apple green*, which turns up in historical lists of color names. Baty reproduces several historical color-name lists that include apple-green, one of them dated 1816 [2]. Among the flower-painter's manuals she discusses, Brookshaw's lists 20 names that Syme later reused, including apple green, sap green and grass green [3]. The Pigment Compendium also records a fifteenth-century German source for a yellow made from apple-tree bark, a reminder that the tree gave color before the fruit gave a name [4].

Our graph keeps the two names apart. [[apple-green]] is a separate entry, 14 CIEDE2000 units from this swatch [1].

sections.title: What a green apple meant
sections.body:
Pastoureau, writing on the cultural history of green, notes that in the Middle Ages a green apple was not a poisoned apple, only a sour one [5]. Poison in medieval tales was red or black, which is why the apple in the Snow White type of story stays red [5]. Green potions and ointments came to stand for the devil's work later, as black lost ground [5].

So the green apple's long association with danger is a later idea, not a medieval one [5].

sections.title: Cézanne's green apples
sections.body:
Pastoureau calls [[painter:paul-cezanne|Cézanne]] the painter of apples above all, and says his apples can take any color [6]. Within the green ones he counts hints of nearly every hue, from white and yellow through brown and red to a bit of purple [6]. A green fruit, in other words, is never one paint.

Pastoureau also records that painters' manuals of the nineteenth century gave recipes for landscape greens, such as a spring-leaf green from Prussian blue, chrome yellow, a little zinc white and a touch of vivid pink [6]. Pastoureau calls pink in a green an innovation [6].

sections.title: The swatch is not the history
sections.body:
The ISCC-NBS system reads the screen color `#5EDC1F` as a vivid yellowish green, within CIEDE2000 6.7 of the block center, and its Munsell reading is about 8.8GY 7.7/15 [1]. It is a screen color from a survey, not a measured fruit [1].

For a duller, older neighbor look at [[apple-green]], or at the cooler [[grass-green]] and [[leek-green]], which appear in the same historical name lists [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
No painting in our archive of 23,781 paintings holds this color at 1 percent of the canvas or more, as photographed [7]. That describes the archive, not painting as a whole [7].

The phrase *green apple* itself has a measurable history. In Google Books it rises in the 1910s, peaks around 1920, and climbs back toward that level in the most recent decade we measure [7]. That curve covers the phrase in every sense, fruit included, not only the color [7].

To train the eye, cut a tart apple and a ripe one open on a white plate and compare the skins: the color you want sits on the sharp one.
